source_text: Quid? si eius memoriam cogitemus non rerum intellegibilium, sed harum corporearum. quam et bestiae habere sentiuntur — nam et per loca nota sine errore iumenta pergunt et cubilia sua bestiae repetunt. et canes dominorum suorum corpora recognoscunt et dormientes plerumque in murmurant et in latratum aliquando erumpunt. quod nullo modo possent, nisi in eorum memoria uisarum rerum uel per corpus utcumque sensarum uersarentur imagines — quis digne cogitet, ubi capiantur istae imagines. ubi gestentur uel ubi formentur? si enim non possent esse maiores quam nostri corporis quantitas teneret. diceret aliquis intra ipsa sui corporis spatia. quibus et illa concluditur. has imagines animam figurare atque seruare. nunc uero cum perexiguam terrae partem occupet corpus. inmensarum regionum et caeli ac terrae imagines animus uoluit. quibus cateruatim discedentibus et succedentibus non fit angustus, atque hinc se ostendit non diffusum esse per locos, quia maximorum locorum imaginibus non quasi capitur. sed potius eas capit, non sinu aliquo, sed ni potentiaque ineffabili, qua licet eis et addere quodlibet et detrahere et in angustum eas contrahere et per inmensa expandere et ordinare. ut uelit, et perturbare et multiplicare et ad paucitatem singularitatemue redigere.
thought_title: Memory of bodily things and the mind's power over images
orientation: Augustine is arguing that the mind is not spread out through space, and here he considers memory of bodily things, which even animals have, to show that the mind contains images of vast places without being extended through them.
pass_a_gloss: What? If we think of its memory not of intelligible things, but of these bodily things, which even beasts are perceived to have — for also through known places beasts of burden proceed without error and beasts repeat their own dens, and dogs recognize the bodies of their own masters and sleeping often murmur and sometimes burst into barking, which they could in no way do unless images of things seen or somehow sensed through the body were moving about in their memory — who worthily thinks where these images are received, where they are carried or where they are formed? For if they could not be greater than the size of our body held, someone would say that within the very spaces of its own body, by which also that body is enclosed, the soul forms and preserves these images. But now, since the body occupies a very small part of the earth, the mind rolls through images of immense regions and of heaven and earth, by which images departing and succeeding in crowds it is not made narrow, and from this it shows itself not to be spread out through places, because by images of the greatest places it is not, as it were, captured, but rather captures them, not by some fold, but by a force and ineffable power, by which it is permitted to it both to add whatever it wishes and to take away and to contract them into a narrow space and to expand them through immense spaces and to arrange them as it wishes, and to disturb them and to multiply them and to reduce them to fewness or singleness.

choices.why: The adjective is substantival, referring back to bodily realities as opposed to intelligible ones; 'bodily things' keeps the contrast with 'intelligible things' explicit.
The passive of uersor suggests images being present and active within memory, not merely stored; 'moving about' preserves the dynamic sense.
In the first occurrence, capio has the sense of taking in or receiving images into memory; 'received' fits the question about where images are taken in.
Sinus here means a hollow or fold as a container; 'fold' preserves the spatial metaphor Augustine is denying.

choices.english: by a force and ineffable power
choices.why: The hendiadys-like pairing emphasizes the mind's non-spatial capacity; keeping both nouns preserves the rhetorical weight.

choices.english: to reduce them to fewness or singleness
choices.why: The abstract nouns paucitas and singularitas are deliberately philosophical; rendering them as abstract nouns keeps Augustine's register.
rejected: to reduce them to a few or to one
to make them few or single

pass_b_english: What if we think of memory not of intelligible things but of these bodily things? Even beasts are perceived to have this kind of memory. Beasts of burden travel without error through places they know, and wild animals return to their dens. Dogs recognize the bodies of their masters, and when asleep they often murmur and sometimes burst into barking. They could not do any of this unless images of things seen or somehow sensed through the body were moving about in their memory. Who can worthily conceive where these images are received, where they are carried, or where they are formed? If they could not be larger than the size of our body allows, someone might say that the soul forms and preserves these images within the very spaces of its own body, in which she too is enclosed. But as it is, though the body occupies a very small part of the earth, the mind ranges through images of immense regions of heaven and earth. As these images depart and succeed one another in crowds, the mind is not made narrow by them. Here it shows itself not to be spread out through places, because it is not, so to speak, contained by images of the largest places, but rather contains them—not by some fold, but by ineffable power by which it can add anything to them and take anything away, contract them into a narrow space, expand them through immensity, arrange them as it wills, throw them into disorder, multiply them, and reduce them to fewness or singleness.

problems.why: Ni is ablative of nisus 'effort/striving,' not 'force'; two distinct nouns, not hendiadys.

edits.old: by a force and ineffable power

fixed: Changed 'by a force and ineffable power' to 'by effort and ineffable power': source 'ni potentiaque ineffabili' has two distinct nouns, nisus (effort/striving) and potentia (power), not a hendiadys.

problems.why: ni is not 'effort' but 'not' (nisi/nihil); should be 'not by some fold, but by ineffable power' or similar
problems.fix: not by some fold, but by ineffable power

edits.old: not by some fold, but by effort and ineffable power
edits.new: not by some fold, but by ineffable power

fixed: Changed 'by effort and ineffable power' to 'by ineffable power': source 'sed ni potentiaque ineffabili' has 'ni' as a negative particle, not 'effort'; the phrase means 'not by some fold, but by ineffable power.'

problems.quote: by which it is also enclosed
problems.why: Illa refers to anima (soul), not ipsa; 'it' should be 'she' or 'the soul,' and the relative quibus refers to spatia (spaces), not the body.
problems.fix: in which she too is enclosed

edits.old: by which it is also enclosed
edits.new: in which she too is enclosed

fixed: Corrected 'by which it is also enclosed' to 'in which she too is enclosed': the source 'quibus et illa concluditur' has 'illa' referring to the soul (anima), and 'quibus' referring to the spaces (spatia), so the soul is enclosed in those spaces, not the body.

dismissed.quote: but by ineffable power by which it can add anything to them and take anything away
dismissed.why: 'ni' is likely a corruption of 'in' or part of 'sinu aliquo, in potentiaque'; as rendered, 'but by...power' drops the negative.
dismissed.note: 'ni' is a scan error for 'ui' (by force), giving 'not by some fold but by force and ineffable power'; there is no negation, so 'but by ineffable power' is right.
